description: Landing on the Moon’s South Pole is tricky—one shadow can freeze a rover, and one hill can block Earth’s signal. We’re Selene Vector 301 (named after the Moon's NASA ID!), a team from Uberlândia building an intuitive, visual "cosmic GPS" to map safe lunar landing windows. Looking for creative devs, designers, and space fans to join our crew!
summary: Planning a landing at the Lunar South Pole is tough: low Sun angles cast long shadows, and nearby ridges can easily block Direct-to-Earth (DTE) radio signals. Existing tools like JPL Horizons and LRO Quickmap hold the answers, but jumping between raw ephemeris tables and heavy terrain maps makes rapid comparison slow. We built Selene Vector 301 to bring those pieces together in one interactive web app. By combining 360° LRO/LOLA horizon elevation profiles and a synchronized 3D lunar globe with NASA JPL Horizons Sun and Earth ephemeris data, the app tracks solar power potential, Earth’s libration wobble, and real-time Sunset and Earthset countdowns on an airless Moon. An AHP-TOPSIS ranking model—tuned to Canadian Space Agency (CSA) rover limits like a 15° max slope and shadow battery life—lets engineers, students, and space fans compare candidate craters or test launch delays in seconds.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

Trying to figure out if a spot near the lunar South Pole actually gets enough sunlight or a clear line of sight to Earth is surprisingly tedious. Normally, you have to cross-reference raw JPL Horizons ephemeris tables with massive elevation maps just to answer a basic question: how long until the Sun drops behind a crater rim?

We built Selene Vector 301 to put those answers on one screen. It combines a 360° polar horizon radar, a synchronized 3D lunar globe, and a multi-criteria site comparison tool so you can test landing sites and launch delays in seconds.

Under the hood, four pieces work together:

- 360° Terrain-Aware Horizon Map: We extracted 72-sector horizon elevation profiles (every 5° of azimuth) and local slope data from NASA LRO/LOLA and LROC Quickmap for 10 sites—nine South Pole Artemis III and CLPS candidates, plus Apollo 11 in Mare Tranquillitatis as a familiar equatorial baseline. Users can also enter any custom Moon coordinates to test spots outside our curated list using an analytical spherical horizon.

- 3D Lunar Orbital Twin: Built with Three.js, the 3D globe syncs real lunar surface imagery with the moving day/night terminator, Sun and Earth direction vectors, and timeline playback (1x, 5x, 20x) across a 336-hour (14-Earth-day) mission window.

- Airless Line-of-Sight Physics: Since the Moon has no atmosphere to bend light or radio signals, our math checks the exact step where the Sun or Earth clears the surrounding crater ridges. This captures Earth's figure-8 libration wobble near the horizon and powers live T-Minus Sunset and Earthset countdowns, <12h warnings, and rover battery State-of-Charge tracking.

- AHP-TOPSIS Ranking & Side-by-Side Comparison: An interactive multi-criteria scoring engine ranks sites by solar uptime, Direct-to-Earth (DTE) radio windows, longest continuous eclipse, ground slope, and distance to water-ice Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs). Users can pin up to two sites next to their active target in Compare Sites to inspect exact deltas and 336-hour timeline bars side by side.

Engineering Choices & Trade-Offs

Rendering raw 3D Digital Elevation Models straight in a browser usually bogs down or crashes regular laptops. Turning 3D crater rims into lightweight 1D horizon silhouettes—and pairing them with precomputed JPL Horizons ephemeris tables (TARGET='301', APPARENT=AIRLESS, 2-hour intervals)—kept recalculations instant at 60 FPS without waiting on a backend server.

We also wired real hardware constraints from the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) lunar rover program into the logic, automatically flagging slopes steeper than 15° and tracking whether rover batteries survive long crater shadows. Because a trajectory engineer and a high school student look for very different things, we split the UI into two modes: Flight Director gives engineers raw Azimuth/Elevation telemetry, weight sliders, launch delay buttons (+7d, +14d, +30d), and CSV/JSON exports, while Explorer swaps heavy jargon for plain-English survival notes (such as -170°C lunar night cold-soak risks) and one-click guided experiments.

Why It Matters

Launch dates slip and lander specs change all the time. When a mission shifts by even a week, science teams chasing PSR water ice and engineering teams needing steady solar power and radio links have to re-check their options fast. Selene Vector 301 makes those trade-offs obvious at a glance—and gives teachers and space fans a straightforward way to see why landing on the lunar South Pole is so tricky.

Tech Stack & NASA Data

Built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js (WebGL), custom SVG polar charts, and Vitest, hosted on Vercel. Powered by NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris data (TARGET='301', APPARENT=AIRLESS), NASA LRO/LOLA & LROC Quickmap elevation masks, NASA Moon Trek, and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) rover mobility parameters.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI) Disclosure

Super Intelligence (SI) tools were used during development to assist with TypeScript/Three.js code scaffolding, debugging, orbital geometry verification, and technical writing refinement. All ephemeris tables, horizon elevation masks, physics calculations, and live demo video/audio recordings were deterministically computed or recorded directly without AI-generated media.
